strengths: Novel technical contribution: First to extend speculative decoding to continuous-valued AR models, addressing a meaningful gap in acceleration techniques for image generation
Mathematically sound derivation: Proper handling of continuous probability distributions, PDF ratios, and Gaussian decomposition with well-justified acceptance criteria and upper bounds

Comprehensive problem-solving approach: Systematically addresses challenges including trajectory divergence, low acceptance rates, and computational intractability through multiple coordinated techniques
Thorough ablation studies: Tables 3-4 provide detailed analysis of trajectory alignment effectiveness, pre-filling ratios, and model pair combinations across different settings
Practical speedups maintained quality: Achieves up to 2.38× acceleration on ImageNet 256×256 with FID/IS metrics comparable to baselines, useful for practitioners
Extensive qualitative validation: Figures 17-21 demonstrate consistent high-quality generation across diverse object categories at different draft lengths
Clear presentation and well-structured exposition: Effective use of diagrams (Figures 2-4) to convey method mechanics; generally accessible writing for the target audience
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: Only ImageNet 256×256 evaluated; no exploration of other resolutions, datasets, domains, or model architectures beyond MAR (GVIT, DiscoART, others mentioned but not compared)
High speedup variability and model-dependency: Results range from 1.13–2.38× with most gains at 1.3–1.7×; no principled framework for draft/target pair selection, requiring empirical testing

Acceptance rate decay limits scalability: Figure 8 shows rapid acceptance ratio decline with draft length; pre-filling (5-15%) feels like a patch that adds inference overhead, reducing effective speedup if properly counted
Missing critical baselines: No comparisons with Jacobi decoding, temperature-based sampling, or other parallel decoding strategies mentioned in related work; limits assessment of relative merit
Theoretical analysis gaps: No convergence characterization, loose bound validation (M=1/Z may be inefficient), or analytical speedup guarantees; entirely empirical framework
Denoising trajectory alignment under-motivated: Ad-hoc post-hoc design without formal justification; no exploration of whether jointly-trained models could have aligned trajectories by design
Quality evaluation limited to standard metrics: Only FID/IS reported without statistical significance testing, user studies, or error analysis of degradation modes at different speedup levels
Reproducibility concerns: Code not provided at review time; implementation details scattered across main paper and appendix; unclear MAR checkpoint specifications
Restricted applicability: Only works for continuous AR models; does not generalize to discrete token models, other AR variants, or demonstrated on other vision domains

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Limited guidance on hyperparameter selection (draft length γ, pre-filling ratios); batch-size sensitivity (1.18× speedup at batch 256) concerning for production; bound tightness and rejection rate characteristics unexplored

strengths: Sound mathematical framework for adapting speculative decoding to continuous distributions, with rigorous derivation of acceptance criteria using probability density ratios
Demonstrates practical speedup (2.33×) on real models with maintained generation quality (FID/IS metrics)
Comprehensive ablation studies examining trajectory alignment, pre-filling, acceptance rates, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Clear problem formulation and effective visual presentation of the core technical challenge (Figure 3)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily an engineering adaptation of existing speculative decoding to continuous space using standard probability theory, without fundamentally new concepts
Severely constrained experimental evaluation: only tested on one model family (MAR), one dataset (ImageNet 256×256), and single GPU - claims about generalizability are not substantiated

Missing critical baselines and comparisons with alternative acceleration methods (distillation, pruning, quantization), making it impossible to assess relative merit or justify the architectural overhead of running two models

Fundamental unresolved problem: acceptance rate decays sharply with draft length (Figure 8, 0.40→0.15), limiting speedup. The proposed 5% pre-filling solution is unprincipled and feels like a workaround
Modest practical impact: 2.33× speedup requires doubled memory and complex dual-model setup. No analysis showing this outperforms simpler alternatives (single smaller model)
Incremental component contributions: trajectory alignment provides only 0.1-0.3 gains (Table 3); pre-filling ratio chosen empirically without principled optimization
Limited quality evaluation: relies primarily on FID/IS metrics with only qualitative visual examples; lacks perceptual studies or user evaluations to support 'quality preservation' claims
Incomplete technical analysis: Figure 5 (modified distribution) underdeveloped; computational costs of acceptance-rejection sampling vs. direct sampling not analyzed; upper bound M effects unclear
Hyperparameter selection lacks justification: draft model pairing criteria unclear, pre-filling ratio arbitrary, temperature sensitivity shown but without actionable guidance

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Identifies and articulates the genuine gap between discrete and continuous speculative decoding, with well-motivated technical challenges

Rigorous mathematical framework: Solid derivation of the acceptance criterion for continuous distributions (Equations 1-11), with thoughtful handling of intractable integrals through modified PDF approximations
Meaningful practical impact: Achieves 2.38× speedup while maintaining output quality (consistent FID/IS metrics), with no architectural modifications required for integration
Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies examining draft length, pre-filling ratios, trajectory alignment effectiveness, and temperature effects with consistent results
Well-designed technical solutions: The acceptance criterion derivation and denoising trajectory alignment strategy are technically sound and represent solid engineering contributions
Strong supplementary materials: Detailed proofs, implementation algorithms, and extensive qualitative results support reproducibility and understanding
weaknesses: Limited novelty and incrementalism: The core contribution is a relatively straightforward adaptation of existing speculative decoding to continuous distributions; individual components (acceptance-rejection sampling, trajectory alignment, pre-filling) lack innovation

Narrow experimental scope: Tested only on MAR model family at single resolution (256×256); no evidence of generalization to other continuous AR models, higher resolutions, or comparison with alternative acceleration methods
Unvalidated approximations: The Gaussian approximation for conditional distributions (Eq. 2) is assumed but not validated; sensitivity to this modeling choice and its impact on results unexplored

Theoretical gaps in key components: The upper bound M = 1/Z is set pragmatically without analysis of sensitivity; the optimal 5% pre-filling ratio lacks theoretical justification; trajectory alignment appears heuristic rather than principled

Incomplete experimental analysis: Acceptance rate variance not addressed; actual measured wall-time speedups not comprehensively validated; memory overhead of maintaining draft/target models not analyzed; no systematic study of failure modes

Missing critical comparisons: No comparison with related acceleration methods (BiLD, distillation, quantization) mentioned in related work; no evaluation on other continuous AR model families or datasets beyond ImageNet

Limited practical guidance: Unclear when practitioners would prefer this method over alternatives; trade-offs between complexity and gains not discussed; computational cost of numerical integration in Eq. 6 not quantified

strengths: First systematic study of continuous speculative decoding for autoregressive image generation with clear problem formulation distinguishing challenges from discrete LLM setting
Novel theoretical contributions including Theorem 1 (proximity in reparameterization reduces distance) and Corollary 1 (easy-to-compute rejection thresholds) with formal proofs

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (MAR, xAR, Harmon) at different resolutions with thorough ablation studies examining trajectory alignment, pre-filling, and batch size effects
Practical design that works without retraining on existing models and seamlessly integrates into three different continuous AR architectures
Strong quantitative and qualitative results with 2.0-2.7× speedup while maintaining FID/IS scores, supported by extensive visualization and detailed ablations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—primarily an engineering adaptation of existing speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023) to continuous distributions rather than a fundamental algorithmic advance

Modest practical improvements (2.0-2.7× speedup, sometimes only 1.11-1.30× at small batch sizes) with acceptance rates remaining low (5-30% even after optimization), suggesting unresolved fundamental limitations

Theoretical assumptions rely on specific Gaussian distribution properties; generality to other continuous distributions unclear, and the connection between trajectory alignment and acceptance rate improvements could be more rigorously established
Narrow application scope limited to autoregressive image generation on ImageNet datasets; generalization to other continuous AR modalities or domains not validated despite broader claims
Requires dual-model deployment (draft + target), significantly increasing memory and infrastructure complexity; the 2× speedup trade-off against this complexity is under-explored

Pre-filling strategy (5% oracle tokens) appears to be a workaround for fundamental low acceptance rates rather than a principled solution; very low initial acceptance rates suggest the core approach struggles
Limited comparison with alternative acceleration methods (distillation, pruning, quantization) and other recent continuous AR acceleration approaches
Dense mathematical presentation in Section 3 could benefit from clearer intuitive explanations, and connection between theoretical results and practical improvements could be more transparent

strengths: Addresses a practical problem of accelerating continuous AR models for image generation
Solid theoretical contributions with formal proofs (Theorem 1 on trajectory alignment, Corollary 1 on rejection threshold)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (MAR, xAR, Harmon) and resolutions
Thorough ablation studies examining contributions of key components (Table 4, 5, 9)
Clear methodology presentation with detailed appendices
Code availability supports reproducibility

No comparison with alternative acceleration methods (knowledge distillation, quantization, other speculative decoding variants, discrete AR approaches)
Insufficient analysis of when practitioners should use this vs. other acceleration techniques

Batch size dependency severely limits practical deployment scenarios
Pre-filling contribution not properly isolated—Table 5 results ambiguous about its relative importance

strengths: Novel contribution: First systematic extension of speculative decoding to continuous autoregressive models with theoretical justification through denoising trajectory alignment
Strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 rigorously proves that trajectory alignment reduces expected inter-sample distance, with formal proofs in appendices
Comprehensive experimental validation: Tests across three models (MAR, xAR, Harmon) at multiple resolutions with extensive ablations on draft length, pre-filling, and temperature effects
Practical speedups demonstrated: Achieves 2×-2.54× wall-time improvements on real hardware (A100) while maintaining generation quality (FID/IS metrics)
Excellent presentation: Clear problem motivation, intuitive visualizations (Figures 2-5), and rich qualitative results across diverse image categories
Seamless integration: Method requires no architectural changes to existing models and can be applied to multiple continuous AR models
Reproducibility: Implementation details thoroughly documented in appendices with code availability promised
weaknesses: Acceptance rate instability: Initial acceptance rates extremely low (~5% at γ=32), non-monotonic relationship with draft length unexplained, requires careful tuning of pre-filling ratios
Incomplete comparisons: Missing comparisons with other acceleration methods (alternative speculative decoding variants, distillation, smaller draft models alone) and concurrent work
Limited theoretical-practical connection: Theorem 1 bounds expected distance but doesn't directly characterize speedup properties or explain acceptance rate behavior in practice
Modest absolute speedup: 2× improvement is incremental; heavily dependent on batch size; single-sample generation shows minimal gains; simpler alternatives might suffice for many applications
Distribution preservation not empirically validated: Claims of preserving original distribution (Appendix A.3) rely only on indirect FID/IS proxies; no human evaluation or perceptual metrics
Scope limitations: Only image generation tested despite claims about audio/video; limited resolution range (256-512); no analysis of model properties determining suitability
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Temperature effects significant (Section G.3); non-trivial guidance provided for practitioners selecting hyperparameters on new models
Computational overhead incomplete analysis: Memory consumption of dual models, overhead of trajectory alignment calculations, and single-GPU evaluation not thoroughly profiled
